Slides of the SURG 453 lecture (black), the doctor's spoken notes from the recording and the previous lecturer's notes (green), every gift (red — this is the most-examined midterm topic, ~200 questions) and the Aldughaither summaries (grey, at the end: acute abdomen + appendix). The previous year's lecture (Dr. Reem Alyahya) is merged in where it adds content.

  • Learning objectives: neuroanatomical pathways of visceral, somatic (parietal) and referred pain · differentiate them by mechanism and character · mechanisms of referred pain (e.g. shoulder-tip pain) · relate site, character and radiation to the organ · approach to the patient with an acute abdomen.

Pain physiology

TypeDefinition (slide)Examples (doctor)
NociceptiveActual or threatened damage to body tissues (gross injury or inflammation)Fracture (direct damage), arthritis (inflammatory)
NeuropathicDamage or dysfunction in the nervous system — the tissue is fineDiabetic neuropathy, shingles (virus in the nerve root)
NociplasticAltered nervous system function without clear tissue damage or a peripheral causeFibromyalgia, migraine — multimodal treatment (psychology/psychiatry + drugs)

Nociceptive · neuropathic · nociplastic pain

Nociceptors

  • Nociceptor = a specialized sensory neuron that detects actual or potential tissue-damaging stimuli and sends threat signals to the spinal cord and brain. Triggers: inflammation, ischaemic damage.

Nociceptor and the mediators that activate it

  • Free nerve endings everywhere, most concentrated in fingertips and toes. Tissue damage → prostaglandins (and bradykinin); inflammation → IL-1, TNF; acute inflammation/abscess → IL-6 → hypothalamus → fever; ischaemia → H⁺ ("any ischaemia will have acidosis").
FibreMyelinSpeedWherePain
AδThinly myelinated5–30 m/sSkin & parietal peritoneumSharp, immediate, well localized
CUnmyelinated0.5–2 m/sAlmost the only fibre in visceraDull, burning, aching, lingers
  • Myelinated → faster → better localization. Viscera are supplied almost only by C fibres → visceral pain is vague.
Key idea: the dorsal horn is where visceral and somatic signals meet (convergence) — this one anatomical fact explains referred pain.
  • 3-order neurons: nociceptor (1st order; Aδ or C; cell body in the dorsal root ganglion; sensitized by prostaglandins, bradykinin, H⁺) → dorsal horn (2nd order; convergence & gating) → crosses the midline, ascends in the spinothalamic tract → thalamus (VPL; 3rd order) → cortex (somatosensory = where; limbic = how much it hurts).

The peritoneum & pain pathways

Understanding the peritoneum — which organs are covered?

  • A huge, permeable membrane (why peritoneal dialysis works); absorbs through stomata under the diaphragm — "a great filter" for bacteria and toxins (~500 mL–1 L/h was audible). Innermost layer of the abdominal wall; parietal + visceral layers; organs are intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal.

  • Surgical pearl: the peritoneum heals extremely fast — an intraperitoneal suture line only needs to hold ~5–7 days before it seals.
  • Dermatome landmarks: xiphoid = T7 · umbilicus = T10 · inguinal ligament = L1.
  • "The most important thing is that you know the landmarks." Lower limb = L2–L5.

Somatic (parietal) pathway — the precise route

  • Supplies: skin, muscles and fascia of the abdominal wall · parietal peritoneum · mesenteric root · periphery of the diaphragm.
  • Nerves: anterior wall — thoracoabdominal T7–T11, subcostal T12, iliohypogastric & ilioinguinal L1; central diaphragm — phrenic C3–C5.
  • Why precise: myelinated Aδ fibres · one side, one dermatome · dense receptor field · point-to-point cortical map.
The parietal peritoneum hurts like skin: sharp, localized, lateralized, worse with movement.

Visceral pathway — the vague route (embryology)

SegmentArteryPlexusOrgans
ForegutCoeliacT5–T9 coeliacOesophagus → 2nd part of duodenum + liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen
MidgutSMAT10–T11 SMADistal duodenum → proximal ⅔ transverse colon + appendix
HindgutIMAT12–L2 IMADistal ⅓ transverse colon → upper rectum
Midline visceral pain tells you the embryological segment, not the organ: epigastric = foregut, periumbilical = midgut, suprapubic = hindgut.
  • The appendix is midgut (SMA) → early appendicitis is periumbilical; it ends in the RIF when the inflamed appendix touches the parietal peritoneum (somatic pathway takes over).
  • Early appendicitis pain is periumbilical because the appendix is midgut. Gift
  • The appendicular artery arises from the ileocolic artery (SMA). Gift
  • SMA thrombosis → ischaemia of the small intestine, caecum and ascending colon ×5; thrombosis causing ischaemia of jejunum, ileum and caecum → SMA. ×2

Visceral, parietal & referred pain

VisceralSomatic / parietalReferred
OriginOrgan wall, capsule, mesenteryParietal peritoneum, abdominal wallVisceral (or deep somatic) source
Fibre & routeC fibres with sympathetic/splanchnic nervesAδ in segmental spinal nervesConvergence on a shared dorsal-horn neuron
LocalizationVague, midline, flat palmPrecise, lateral, one fingerDistant dermatome, normal-looking site
CharacterDull, cramping, colickySharp, constant, stabbingAching or sharp; may be hyperaesthetic
BehaviourRestless, writhing, nauseatedLies still; hurts to move or coughRubs or points to the referral site
ExaminationLittle or no local tendernessTenderness, guarding, rebound, rigidityNo tenderness at the referral site
Classic exampleEarly appendicitis, bowel or ureteric colicLate appendicitis, perforated ulcerShoulder tip from diaphragm; scapula from gallbladder
  • Visceral triggers: stretch/distension of a hollow viscus, smooth-muscle spasm, ischaemia, inflammation, traction on the mesentery. Autonomic signs: nausea, vomiting, sweating, pallor, bradycardia.
  • Parietal triggers: inflammation reaching the parietal peritoneum; blood, pus, bile, gastric or bowel content touching it; direct abdominal wall injury. Patient lies still, shallow breaths; tenderness, guarding, rebound, percussion tenderness, rigidity when generalized.

Referred pain

  • Pain felt at a site distant from its source, in the dermatome supplied by the same spinal segment as the diseased organ.
Migrating ≠ radiating ≠ referred. Migrating = starts in one place then moves (appendicitis: umbilicus → RIF). Radiating = spreads from the source at the same time (retrosternal → left arm). Referred = felt at a distant normal-looking site (dorsal-horn convergence).
  • Shoulder-tip pain: irritant under the central diaphragm (blood, pus, free air, bile, CO₂) → phrenic nerve C3–C5 → dorsal horn C3–C4 shared with the supraclavicular nerves → skin of the shoulder tip.
Kehr's sign (shoulder-tip pain) causes: ruptured spleen (blood) · ruptured ectopic pregnancy (blood) · perforated ulcer (free air) · subphrenic abscess · after laparoscopy — CO₂ (benign).
  • In a woman with Kehr's sign, ask about the last period. CO₂ is used for laparoscopy (non-flammable, rapidly absorbed).
  • The peripheral diaphragm is different: supplied by intercostal nerves T6–T12 → lower chest/upper abdominal wall pain → basal pneumonia or pleurisy can present as "abdominal pain".

  • Previous lecture — SOCRATES: site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms, time course, exacerbating/relieving factors, severity. Onset: "sharp pain that started 4 hours ago" vs "on/off pain for 4 months". Chief complaint = 1–2 complaints with age, sex, duration (e.g. 16-year-old + RLQ pain × 5 h → appendicitis likely). Important negatives = symptoms asked to exclude complications/differentials (RUQ pain → ask about jaundice, urine and stool colour).
  • Do not miss: epigastric pain can be an MI. Duration changes the differential: intermittent RUQ pain over months → biliary colic; continuous for a day → cholecystitis.

Approach to the acute surgical abdomen

  • What is an acute abdomen? — a huge differential (the slide lists ~80 causes: surgical, medical, gynaecological, urological, metabolic — e.g. DKA, adrenal crisis, porphyria, sickle cell, pneumonia, herpes zoster, lead poisoning).
  • Previous lecture: severe persistent abdominal pain likely to require surgical intervention; "surgical abdomen" doesn't always mean an operation. Not all acute abdominal pain is general-surgical — the first job may be surgical vs non-surgical triage. Non-GS causes: lower-lobe pneumonia, gastroenteritis, ectopic/ovarian torsion, renal stones, testicular torsion, DKA, hypothyroidism, drugs/toxins.
Five mechanisms: 1. inflammation · 2. perforation · 3. obstruction · 4. ischaemia · 5. haemorrhage.
  • Don't think of the diagnosis first. The first question: "Is this patient going to die or not?" Recognize the acute abdomen, decide if it is life-threatening, then think through the five mechanisms. Acute = sudden + severe.

Step 1 — Recognize

  • Appearance (well / ill / sick) · Cognition (conscious / confused) · Stability (vitally stable / unstable).
  • First: don't touch — look. "If he looks confused, he is confused" — in this setting confusion = shock. Stability = mainly HR and BP.
Well + conscious + stableIll/sick + confused + unstable

Focused examinationResuscitation, bedside tests & labs
Targeted investigationsSelective imaging; recognize the type of shock
Provisional/working diagnosisShort history, focused exam
Management & dispositionReassess, reassess, reassess → disposition (OR or ICU)
  • Responding to resuscitation → carry on; not responding → something is wrong → OR or ICU.
"Recognize" icons (3)
  • Severe pain, guarding, rigidity, sepsis, haemodynamically unstable → emergency laparotomy. 442
  • RIF pain that became generalized, HR > 120, generalized distension and tenderness → first IV fluids (resuscitate before anything). Gift
  • Pain, vomiting, distension, hyperactive bowel sounds, normal vitals → first IV fluids. Gift

The resuscitation bundle

Close monitoring · 2 large-bore IV + labs · IV fluids · blood (if needed) · broad-spectrum antibiotics · urine catheter · NG tube (if needed) · steroids (if needed). You must state the whole bundle — steroids are the "advanced" point.
  • Close monitoring: connect to a monitor, 12-lead ECG (not a one-off set of vitals).
  • Labs: blood sugar · blood gas (ABG/VBG) · CBC · electrolytes · urea & creatinine · lactate · LFTs · amylase & lipase · cross-match · urinalysis + culture · β-hCG (female of childbearing age) · blood culture — please!
  • Lactate: high = global hypoperfusion (shock) or local ischaemia (twisted bowel). Amylase/lipase always in sick patients. Cross-match because you don't yet know the cause (haemorrhage, resection). Bedside tests: ECG, urinalysis, blood sugar, β-hCG.
  • Blood if haemorrhagic shock is suspected (e.g. haematemesis) — uncross-matched if cross-matched isn't ready.
  • Antibiotics (broad-spectrum): cover common Gram-positive and Gram-negative — e.g. vancomycin (MRSA) + an anti-pseudomonal β-lactam (cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam). Do not start before withdrawing BLOOD CULTURE!
  • Antibiotics in all five mechanisms: inflammation/perforation = infection; obstruction = bacterial translocation. Blood culture takes ~5 minutes.
  • Urine catheter: guides resuscitation — normal urine output 0.5–1 mL/kg/h; send urinalysis and culture.
  • NG tube (if needed): all patients with suspected obstruction — decompression, connect to suction; confused patients — prevent aspiration.
  • Best tube: Salem sump — 2 lumens (suction + blue vent lumen).
  • Steroids (if needed): chronic steroid use or suspected adrenal insufficiency → stress dose 100 mg hydrocortisone IV.
  • He described a patient thought to be in haemorrhagic shock who was actually in adrenal crisis.
  • Myth: "Don't give analgesia, it masks the signs." Withholding analgesia makes the exam less reliable — a patient in agony can't relax the abdominal wall. Treat the pain, then examine — analgesia doesn't obscure peritoneal signs or delay diagnosis.
Myth vs evidence icons (2)
  • Correct about the NG tube → aspirate gastric content (to confirm position) Gift; during NG intubation → keyed auscultation to confirm placement Gift; why insert an NGT on the ward → GI bleeding Gift; indication for NGT → perforated duodenal ulcer (skull-base/maxillofacial fractures are contraindications). Gift
  • Septic shock after laparotomy for a perforated DU with purulent peritonitis → characterized by peripheral vasodilation. ×2

Selective imaging

  • Upright CXR · abdominal X-ray series (standing, supine, lateral decubitus) — always start with them · ultrasound · CT · MRI.
  • Plain films before CT. Upright/semi-sitting CXR → air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum). Abdominal series: supine, upright, lateral decubitus. Inconclusive → US (e.g. gallbladder). Once stable → CT (or MRI).
Stable patient + free air under the diaphragm = perforation → exploratory laparotomy.
  • Stable + dilated loops with air-fluid levels = obstruction → still needs history & physical exam to decide.
Imaging (build-up) (2)
  • Severe pain with rigidity, guarding and rebound → first imaging upright chest X-ray. ×2
  • Imaging when evaluating suspected bowel perforation → plain X-ray ×3; elderly patient with an acute abdomen → keyed chest X-ray (plain films first). 436
  • Sudden severe epigastric pain → erect chest X-ray first 432 ×3 429 Gift Gift; DU patient on aspirin, sudden pain, generalized guarding → erect CXR. ×4
  • Epigastric pain + raised amylase → initial investigation still erect CXR (exclude perforation — it can raise amylase) 436; tip from the recalls: any pancreatitis-like scenario where no erect X-ray was done → erect X-ray is the answer. 435
  • Air under the diaphragm already seen → don't repeat imaging; resuscitate and operate. 434
  • X-ray after sudden epigastric pain → perforated viscus 435 ×2; the same free-air film in a patient with fever and shortness of breath → still perforated viscus, not pneumonia 435 Gift
  • AF + IHD with acute abdomen → keyed CT abdomen (suspected mesenteric ischaemia). Gift
  • Admitted 30 minutes ago with acute RUQ pain → initial investigation keyed CBC. Gift

Focused history & examination

  • History: pain analysis — focus mainly on onset and severity (they separate the urgent causes), then site, character, radiation.
  • Exam: full abdominal exam — all 9 regions · check hernia orifices — please! · DRE — please! ×10.
  • Missing the hernia orifices and DRE is a classic way to lose marks. Look for guarding and rigidity.
  • Previous lecture: history → exam → labs (CBC, LFT, U&E, coagulation, amylase, hCG) and imaging (X-ray, US, CT) → scopes (endoscopy, colonoscopy, diagnostic laparoscopy) → rule out common, then life-threatening pathologies. RLQ pain → rule out appendicitis; epigastric pain → exclude MI; woman of reproductive age → exclude pregnancy/ectopic.

Mechanism 1 — Haemorrhage

  • CT: bleeding with the density of the aorta = arterial; of the IVC = venous. Portal hypertension → thin-walled collaterals (lower oesophagus, rectum, umbilicus) → massive bleeding. Mallory–Weiss usually self-limited. Diverticulosis (~50% > 50 y, ~80% > 80 y) is a common cause of lower GI bleeding.

Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

Woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain → β-hCG. RIF/lower pain + amenorrhoea + fainting, tachycardia, hypotension = ruptured ectopic (shoulder tip from blood under the diaphragm).
  • Married lady, cramping RIF pain becoming generalized, fainting, tachycardia → ruptured ectopic pregnancy 429 428 Gift; 19-year-old, 2 months' amenorrhoea, worsening lower abdominal pain → ruptured ectopic. ×3
  • Married 24-year-old, lower abdominal pain, BP 90/60, pulse 120 → the differential that must be excluded → ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Gift
  • Sudden severe RLQ pain in a 24-year-old woman → important test → pregnancy test Gift; missed period, severe pain, tachycardia → next step urinary β-hCG. Gift

Ruptured AAA

  • Hypotensive with a pulsatile epigastric mass → immediate laparotomy (no CT in an unstable rupture). Gift

GI bleeding (from past exams)

  • Rebleeding after a bleeding ulcer — the endoscopic finding that predicted it → adherent clot. Gift
  • Vomiting clear fluid then bright red blood after drinking → Mallory–Weiss tear. Gift
  • Variceal bleed — IV drug proven to reduce mortality → ceftriaxone Gift; cirrhotic vomiting blood, after resuscitation → octreotide. Gift
  • 70-year-old, large painless fresh PR bleeding, shocked → keyed angiodysplasia Gift; painless massive rectal bleeding, NG aspirate shows bile (no blood) → diverticulosis Gift; localize active lower GI bleeding → CT angiography Gift; 70-year-old, blood mixed with stool, constipation, weight loss → colon cancer. Gift

Mechanism 2 — Inflammation

Acute appendicitis

  • Phase 1 = C fibres (diffuse, midline); pain migrates when the appendix touches the parietal peritoneum. Work-up the doctor asked for: β-hCG mandatory in females; differentials ureteric stone, gastroenteritis; CBC (neutrophilia, left shift), CRP, urinalysis, electrolytes, lactate, amylase/lipase.
  • Imaging: US in children, pregnant women and thin patients; CT is the standard in adults — its main job is to exclude other causes. In pregnancy from ~20 weeks the appendix is pushed upward. Surgery: laparoscopic appendectomy.
  • Previous lecture: early appendicitis may have no RIF tenderness — the patient may be sent home and return; if early imaging shows appendicitis → admit and treat. Normal appendix at surgery → inspect the distal ileum for Meckel's diverticulum.
  • Acute appendicitis is diagnosed mainly clinically. 429
  • Pain in the RIF when pressing the LIF = Rovsing's sign Gift 439 429; best indicator of appendicitis → keyed RIF pain on pressing the left side (Rovsing). Gift
  • Suspected appendicitis in an adult, unsure if classical (β-hCG negative) → CT 442; 18-year-old, RLQ pain 18 h with rebound → CT abdomen and pelvis 438 ×2 ×2; RLQ pain 8 h, T 38 → CT 438; RLQ pain 4 days with rebound → CT 438; obese 25-year-old with RLQ pain, high WBC → CT. 434
  • Young woman, periumbilical → RLQ pain, β-hCG normal → keyed US first. Gift
  • 10-year-old with RLQ pain, fever, guarding, high WBC → urgent appendectomy. Gift
  • Typical appendicitis with a RLQ mass → keyed appendectomy. 427
  • RLQ pain 5 days with a tender mass → ultrasound (abscess vs phlegmon). 429
Appendiceal abscess (stable) → IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage (± interval appendectomy). Appendiceal mass treated conservatively in an older patient → colonoscopy to exclude caecal cancer.
  • 3-cm peri-appendiceal abscess → IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage 442 442 441; US shows appendicitis with a large pus collection → drainage. ×3
  • 58-year-old, appendicular mass resolved with conservative treatment → next colonoscopy. 434
  • After laparoscopic appendectomy for perforation: fever + RLQ pain, wound fine → intra-abdominal abscess Gift; persistent fever, RLQ tenderness → antibiotics + percutaneous drainage. Gift 3 weeks after laparotomy, fever and a large intra-abdominal collection → percutaneous drainage. Gift
  • NSAID user: epigastric pain shifting to the RIF, generalized guarding and rigidity → exploratory laparotomy (perforated ulcer tracking down the right paracolic gutter). Gift
  • Incidental appendiceal adenocarcinoma → right hemicolectomy 442; carcinoid < 2 cm, confined, clear margins → appendectomy is sufficient 442; most common appendiceal tumour → carcinoid (neuroendocrine). 441

Acute cholecystitis & cholangitis (from past exams)

Added explanationBiliary disease is taught in the Gallstones lecture; these questions were filed under acute abdomen.
  • Key sign of gallbladder inflammation → Murphy's sign ×2 Gift; most sensitive/specific imaging for acute cholecystitis → ultrasound Gift; RUQ colicky pain 5 days, slight fever → cholecystitis. 438
  • RUQ pain 36 h with right shoulder-tip pain → abdominal US ×7; epigastric/hypochondrial pain, mild icterus, fever, leukocytosis → US 439; RUQ pain, jaundice, dark urine → initial US abdomen 429; fever 39.5 + jaundice for 5 days → transabdominal US. 437
  • Acute cholecystitis → cholecystectomy during the index admission 442 438 439 Gift; after 4 days with fever, thick wall and pericholecystic fluid → best initial management keyed non-interventional (conservative) Gift; 8 days of pain → keyed delayed cholecystectomy in 2–3 months. 435 ×3
  • 95-year-old, poor ASA, acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy 441 441; cholecystitis + choledocholithiasis → ERCP + cholecystectomy. Gift
  • Acalculous cholecystitis — the false statement → "CT is the investigation of choice". Gift
  • Charcot's triad = RUQ pain, fever and jaundice 429 ×3 Gift; symptom linked to the triad (jaundice) → keyed pruritus Gift; fever, jaundice, RUQ pain, tachycardia, cholestatic LFTs → acute cholangitis 442 ×4; RUQ pain, fever, jaundice, itching, dark urine, dilated CBD → cholangitis 438; on Mounjaro, RUQ pain to the shoulder, fever, hypotension, tea-coloured urine → acute cholangitis. Gift
  • Cholangitis — initial management → IV fluids (then antibiotics, then ERCP) 428 429 Gift Gift

Acute pancreatitis (from past exams)

  • Most common cause → gallstones Gift; obese woman with gallstones, continuous mid-abdominal pain → acute pancreatitis 432 ×3; epigastric pain to the back, vomiting → acute pancreatitis ×2; prior cholecystectomy + long alcohol intake → alcoholic pancreatitis Gift; dark flank discolouration → Grey Turner's sign. ×4
  • Initial step with amylase 1246 → IV fluids 429; gallstone pancreatitis → IV crystalloids 438 ×3; mild pancreatitis → enteral feeding, IV fluids, analgesia (no TPN/antibiotics). 441
  • Amylase 1534 / 1854 → imaging → ultrasound (gallstones) 429 ×6; amylase 250 after an erect X-ray → US 435 Gift; amylase 250 and normal CXR → keyed CT 432 ×2; pain for 5 days, amylase only 150 → urine amylase (serum amylase falls early) Gift 435 ×4
  • Pseudocyst — indication for surgery → gastric and duodenal obstruction. Gift

Diverticulitis

Most common site → sigmoid colon. Uncomplicated → IV fluids + antibiotics; pericolic abscess → antibiotics + percutaneous drainage; free perforation/peritonitis → laparotomy (Hartmann's).
  • Most common site of diverticulitis → sigmoid colon. 442
  • Pericolic abscess with localized peritonitis → Hinchey I (keyed "Ia — pericolic or mesenteric abscess"; in the modified scale a pericolic abscess is Ib). 441
  • 5-cm pericolic abscess, stable, no generalized peritonitis → IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage. 442
  • Elderly diabetic with LLQ pain, fever, stable → fluid resuscitation + IV antibiotics 429; CT: thick sigmoid wall, no collection → keyed IV fluid. Gift
  • Known diverticulitis on IV antibiotics, now air under the diaphragm → laparotomy. Gift
  • Diverticula seen in the ileum — true statement → diverticula are acquired. 441

IBD

  • Previous lecture: IBD can present as an acute abdomen; Crohn's may later cause obstruction (stricture).
  • 6 bloody stools, fever, leukocytosis, generalized tenderness (fulminant colitis with peritonitis) → keyed colectomy. Gift
  • Crohn's patient after hemicolectomy, local peritonitis days later → anastomotic leak. Gift

Mechanism 3 — Perforation

  • Free air above the liver/right hemidiaphragm is abnormal (left-sided gas may be the gastric bubble). Pneumoperitoneum is enough to operate; if stable, CT can localize — don't delay.
  • On aspirin, sudden epigastric pain, guarding and resonant percussion over the liver → perforated peptic ulcer 429 428; elderly woman on aspirin with 1 day of pain → peptic ulcer disease 428; arthritis + pneumoperitoneum → perforated PU ×2; NSAID user with perforation → Graham patch. Gift
  • Smoker with severe epigastric pain — confirm (ulcer) → upper GI endoscopy Gift; organism linked to upper GI neoplasia → H. pylori. ×3

Mechanism 4 — Obstruction

  • Small bowel: adhesions · hernias · intussusception · malignancies · functional (pseudo-obstruction). Large bowel: cancer · volvulus · intussusception · diverticular disease. (Examples only — many extraluminal, intraluminal and transmural causes.)
  • He told the class to write notes here — examinable. First question in SBO: has the patient had surgery before? Previous surgery = adhesions. Virgin abdomen = hernia, congenital band, malignancy or intussusception. Large bowel: cancer, volvulus (sigmoid or caecum), diverticular disease in the elderly.
  • Pseudo-obstruction (elderly/ICU, no mechanical cause): avoid opioids → correct electrolytes → neostigmine in ICU → decompression if it fails.

Scenario 1 — adhesive SBO

Acute Abdomen

An acute abdomen refers to sudden, severe, nontraumatic abdominal pain of <24 hours duration requiring urgent evaluation.

  • Many cases require emergency surgery to prevent complications (e.g., peritonitis, sepsis, ischemia).
  • Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to improve outcomes and reduce morbidity/mortality.
Clinical Approach to Acute Abdomen
1. History & Risk Factors

Key Historical Questions:

Onset: Sudden (e.g., perforation, ischemia) vs. gradual (e.g., appendicitis, pancreatitis).

Character: Colicky (obstruction), sharp (perforation), dull (inflammation).

Location & Radiation:

  • RUQ → Cholecystitis, liver abscess
  • RLQ → Appendicitis, Crohn’s disease
  • LLQ → Diverticulitis, sigmoid volvulus
  • Epigastric → Peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, MI Exacerbating/Relieving Factors: Eating, movement, position change, analgesics. Associated Symptoms: Fever, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, weight loss.
2. Physical Examination
  • Critical Exam Findings:
  • Peritonitis (Rebound, Guarding, Rigidity, Absent Bowel Sounds) →
  • Surgical emergency!
  • Palpable mass → Abscess, tumor, aneurysm.
  • Distension → Ileus, bowel obstruction, ascites.
  • Murphy’s Sign (RUQ pain on inspiration) → Cholecystitis.
  • Rovsing’s, Psoas, Obturator Signs → Appendicitis.
  • Cullen’s / Grey Turner’s Signs → Hemorrhagic pancreatitis, ruptured
  • ectopic pregnancy.
III. Laboratory & Imaging Workup
1- Essential Labs
  • Complete Blood Count (CBC) → Leukocytosis (infection, ischemia).
  • Electrolytes & Renal Function → Dehydration, metabolic imbalances.
  • Liver Function Tests (LFTs) → Elevated AST/ALT (hepatobiliary disease).
  • Amylase/Lipase → Pancreatitis.
  • Lactate → Bowel ischemia.
  • Beta-hCG (if female) → Ectopic pregnancy.
2- Diagnostic Imaging
  • Ultrasound (FAST Scan) → Gallstones, cholecystitis, ascites, AAA.
  • X-ray (Upright & Supine Abdomen, Chest X-ray) → Free air (perforation),
  • dilated loops (obstruction).
  • CT Abdomen/Pelvis with IV Contrast → Gold standard for appendicitis,
  • diverticulitis, ischemia, and abscess.
  • MRI → Preferred in pregnancy (appendicitis, biliary pathology).
IV. Management Based on Diagnosis
Surgical Emergencies (Immediate OR)
  • Perforated Viscus → Free air on X-ray/CT, peritonitis → Laparotomy
  • Mesenteric Ischemia → Severe pain, ↑ lactate → Embolectomy or bowel
  • resection
  • Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy → Unstable vitals, +β-hCG → Salpingectomy
  • Strangulated Hernia, Volvulus, Obstructed Bowel → Emergency surgery
Urgent Surgical Cases (Within 24 hours)
  • Appendicitis → CT-confirmed, RLQ pain, leukocytosis → Appendectomy
  • Cholecystitis → US-confirmed gallstones, Murphy’s sign →
  • Cholecystectomy
  • Diverticulitis with Abscess or Perforation → CT-guided drainage, possible
  • sigmoidectomy
Non-Surgical Management
  • Uncomplicated diverticulitis → IV antibiotics, bowel rest.
  • Acute pancreatitis → Fluids, NPO, analgesia, NO antibiotics (unless infected
  • necrosis).
  • Gastroenteritis → Supportive care, hydration, antiemetics.
Abdominal pain:
Location of Pain
  • Key to determining affected organ/system
  • Generalized → Peritonitis, perforation, ischemia.
  • RUQ → Cholecystitis, hepatitis, liver abscess.
  • LUQ → Splenic rupture, pancreatitis, gastric ulcer.
  • RLQ → Appendicitis, Crohn’s disease, ovarian torsion.
  • LLQ → Diverticulitis, sigmoid volvulus.
  • Epigastric → Peptic ulcer disease, pancreatitis, MI.
  • Flank Pain → Renal colic, pyelonephritis.
  • Suprapubic → Cystitis, ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease.
  • Types of Pain Transmission
  • Visceral pain (hollow organ distension, ischemia) → Dull, deep, poorly
  • localized.
  • Parietal pain (peritoneal irritation) → Sharp, localized, worsens with
  • movement.
  • Referred pain (shared nerve pathways) → Pain at a distant site (e.g.,
  • diaphragmatic irritation → shoulder pain).
Mode of Onset & Progression
Sudden, severe pain (Seconds-Minutes)
  • Perforated viscus (peptic ulcer)
  • Aortic dissection or rupture
  • Ovarian torsion, testicular torsion
  • Mesenteric ischemia
Rapidly progressive pain (1-2 hours)
  • Cholecystitis, pancreatitis
  • Appendicitis, diverticulitis
  • Strangulated hernia, bowel ischemia
Gradual, insidious pain (Several hours)
  • Obstruction (small bowel, large bowel)
  • Inflammatory conditions (Crohn’s, ulcerative colitis)
  • Hepatitis, ascites, peritoneal carcinomatosis
Shifting Pain Patterns

Appendicitis: Starts periumbilical → localizes to RLQ.

Perforated ulcer: Starts epigastric → descends RUQ/RLQ.

Character of Pain

Sharp, localized → Peritoneal irritation (e.g., perforated ulcer, peritonitis).

Colicky, cramping → Hollow organ obstruction (e.g., bowel obstruction, ureteric colic).

Burning, gnawing → Peptic ulcer disease, GERD.

Tearing, excruciating → Aortic dissection, ruptured aneurysm.

Stabbing, radiating → Pancreatitis (back), renal colic (groin).

Intermittent pain-free periods → Ureteric colic, biliary colic (not true colic).

Pain worsened by movement → Peritonitis, appendicitis, cholecystitis.

Associated symptoms:
I. Vomiting
Surgical vs. Medical Causes:
  • Acute surgical abdomen: Pain precedes vomiting.
  • Medical conditions (e.g., gastroenteritis): Vomiting precedes pain.
Key Patterns of Vomiting:

Bilious vomiting → Proximal small bowel obstruction.

Feculent vomiting → Distal small bowel or large bowel obstruction.

Projectile, non-bilious vomiting → Pyloric stenosis (infants).

Severe, forceful vomiting → Boerhaave syndrome (esophageal rupture).

Recurrent vomiting with pain relief → Pancreatitis.

Differential Considerations:

Large bowel obstructionLate, feculent vomiting
Gastric outlet obstructionNon-bilious, projectile vomiting
PancreatitisPersistent nausea, sometimes relieves pain
II. Constipation & Obstipation
  • Key Distinctions:
  • Paralytic ileus → Reflex bowel shutdown due to inflammation, trauma, or
  • surgery.
  • Constipation alone → Non-specific but may indicate ileus, chronic
  • obstruction, or dehydration.
  • Obstipation (no stool or gas passage) → Strongly suggests mechanical
  • bowel obstruction.

III. Diarrhea
  • Key Features:
  • Profuse, watery diarrhea → Gastroenteritis, Clostridium difficile infection.
  • Bloody diarrhea → Inflammatory or ischemic conditions (ulcerative colitis,
  • Crohn’s, ischemic colitis).
  • Mucus & blood → Dysentery (bacterial or amebic).
  • Painless diarrhea with weight loss → Malabsorption syndromes (celiac,
  • chronic pancreatitis).
  • Alternating constipation & diarrhea → irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

IV. Fever
Low Sensitivity:
  • Not always present in acute abdomen, especially in immunocompromised patients.
  • Some conditions may present without fever, even with severe inflammation.

V. Other Key Symptoms

Weight Loss → Consider malignancy, chronic mesenteric ischemia, tuberculosis.

Jaundice → Suggests hepatobiliary disease (cholangitis, pancreatic cancer, viral hepatitis).

Hematochezia → Lower GI bleed (diverticulosis, ischemic colitis, colon cancer).

Melena → Upper GI bleed (gastric ulcer, esophageal varices).

Hematuria → Suggests nephrolithiasis, bladder cancer, UTI.

Obstruction
  • Extraluminal: Hernias, volvulus, adhesions
  • Intraluminal: Gallstone ileus, ureteric stone, bezoar
  • Luminal (mural): malignancy, IBD
I. Past Medical History

A complete medical history helps identify pre-existing conditions that may either cause or mimic an acute abdomen.

Key Conditions to Consider:
  • Cardiovascular disease → Atrial fibrillation & vascular disease →
  • Mesenteric ischemia
  • Liver disease → Cirrhosis → Ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
  • (SBP), variceal bleeding
  • Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) → Crohn’s, ulcerative colitis →
  • Strictures, abscesses, obstruction, perforation
  • Diabetes → Gastroparesis → Chronic abdominal pain & vomiting
  • Immunosuppression (HIV, chemotherapy, steroids) → Atypical infections,
  • perforations, masked peritonitis
  • Recent trauma → Delayed splenic rupture, mesenteric injury, bowel
  • hematoma
II. Surgical History

Previous abdominal, vascular, or thoracic surgery is crucial for evaluating complications like:

  • Adhesions → Small bowel obstruction.
  • Previous hernia repair → Recurrent hernia causing obstruction.
  • Gastric surgery → Marginal ulcers, dumping syndrome, malabsorption.
  • Biliary surgery (cholecystectomy) → Post-cholecystectomy syndrome
  • (biliary pain, diarrhea).
  • History of stents, mesh, or implants → Foreign body infections or
  • obstruction.
  • Operative approach (open vs. laparoscopic) → Laparoscopic procedures
  • reduce adhesion formation compared to open surgery.
III. Gynecologic History (for Female Patients)
Menstrual & Obstetric History:
  • Irregular menses, missed period → Suspect ectopic pregnancy.
  • Pain at mid-cycle (mittelschmerz) → Ruptured ovarian follicle.
  • Severe dysmenorrhea & pelvic pain → Endometriosis.
  • Postpartum status, prior C-section → Increased risk for uterine rupture,
  • adhesions, and bowel obstruction.
Gynecological Infections & Pelvic Pain:
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) → Fevers, vaginal discharge, adnexal
  • tenderness.
  • Ovarian torsion → Sudden severe pelvic pain, nausea/vomiting.
IV. Medication History
Common Medications Affecting the Abdomen:
  • NSAIDs/Aspirin → Gastritis, peptic ulcer, perforation.
  • Anticoagulants (Warfarin, DOACs, Heparin) → Retroperitoneal &
  • intramural hematomas, spontaneous bleeding.
  • Corticosteroids, Immunosuppressants → Mask peritonitis, delay sepsis
  • symptoms.
  • Oral contraceptives → Hepatic adenomas, mesenteric venous thrombosis.
  • Opioids → Constipation, ileus, pseudo-obstruction.
  • Diuretics → Electrolyte imbalance, metabolic alkalosis, ileus.
  • Chemotherapy → Neutropenic colitis, enterocolitis.
V. Family History
Hereditary Conditions That Mimic Acute Abdomen:
  • Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) → Recurrent peritonitis, fever,
  • abdominal pain.
  • Hereditary colorectal cancer (HNPCC, FAP) → Increased risk of bowel
  • obstruction, malignancy.
  • Porphyria → Intermittent abdominal pain, neurological symptoms.
  • Hereditary pancreatitis → Recurrent severe abdominal pain &
  • hyperamylasemia.
  • Cystic fibrosis → Meconium ileus in newborns, distal intestinal obstruction
  • syndrome (DIOS) in adults.
VI. Travel History
Geographical Risk Factors for Infectious Causes of Acute Abdomen:
  • Amebic liver abscess → Travel to endemic areas (India, Mexico, Africa,
  • South America).
  • Hydatid cyst (Echinococcus infection) → Contact with sheep, dogs, or
  • travel to Middle East, South America, Mediterranean, Australia.
  • Salmonella typhi (Typhoid fever) → History of travel to South Asia or
  • Africa → Enteric fever, ileocecal perforation.
  • Tuberculosis → Extrapulmonary TB can cause intestinal TB, ileocecal
  • involvement.
  • Malaria → Splenic rupture in endemic regions.
  • Schistosomiasis → Portal hypertension, hepatosplenic disease.
Abdominal examination:
1. Inspection
  • Look for:
    • Surgical scars → Adhesions → Small bowel obstruction (SBO).
    • Hernias → Strangulated/incarcerated hernia → Bowel obstruction.
    • Distension:
    • Tense, tympanitic distension → SBO.
    • Soft, doughy fullness → Ileus, mesenteric ischemia.
    • Visible peristalsis → Late-stage bowel obstruction.
    • Cullen's sign (periumbilical ecchymosis) → Retroperitoneal hemorrhage (pancreatitis, ruptured aneurysm).
    • Grey Turner’s sign (flank ecchymosis) → Retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

2. Auscultation

  • High-pitched rushes & borborygmi → Early obstruction.
  • Absent bowel sounds → Peritonitis, ileus.
  • Bruit → Vascular aneurysm or renal artery stenosis.

3. Percussion

  • Tenderness on percussion → Peritoneal irritation.
  • Dullness in flanks → Ascites (check shifting dullness).
  • Loss of liver dullness → Perforated viscus (free air under diaphragm).

4. Palpation

  • Begin away from the site of maximal pain and gradually move toward it.
  • Localized tenderness → Common in cholecystitis, appendicitis, diverticulitis.
  • Diffuse tenderness → Suggests peritonitis, mesenteric ischemia, pancreatitis.
  • Severe pain out of proportion to exam → Mesenteric ischemia.
  • Rebound tenderness:
    • Pain on quick release → Peritoneal irritation.
    • Can be elicited by bed bumping or shaking the abdomen.
  • Guarding & Rigidity:
    • Voluntary guarding → Pain improves with distraction.
    • Involuntary rigidity ("board-like") → Peritonitis.

5. Masses & Organomegaly

  • Gallbladder distension → Acute cholecystitis.
  • Pulsatile mass → Aortic aneurysm.
  • Deep mass with ill-defined borders → Pancreatic phlegmon, ruptured aneurysm.

Investigations:
A. Blood Tests
1. Complete Blood Count (CBC)
  • Leukocytosis (>13,000/µL) → Suggests infection, inflammation, or perforation.
  • Left shift (neutrophilia, band forms) → Serious bacterial infection.
  • Leukopenia (<5000/µL) → Severe sepsis, viral infection, overwhelming infection.
  • Low hemoglobin/hematocrit → Suggests hemorrhage.
  • Elevated hematocrit → May indicate dehydration or hemoconcentration.

2. Serum Electrolytes, Urea Nitrogen (BUN), and Creatinine

  • Dehydration & shock → Elevated BUN/Creatinine ratio.
  • Hypokalemia → Common in vomiting, diarrhea, bowel obstruction.
  • Hyperkalemia → Possible in mesenteric ischemia or renal failure.

3. Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) and Lactate

  • Metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate → Bowel ischemia, shock, sepsis.
  • Unexplained metabolic acidosis → Early sign of serious intra- abdominal pathology.

4. Pancreatic Enzymes

  • Elevated amylase & lipase → Acute pancreatitis.
  • Moderate amylase elevation → Can be seen in perforated ulcer, ischemic bowel, or ruptured ovarian cyst.

5. Liver Function Tests (LFTs)

  • Elevated bilirubin, AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase → Hepatobiliary disease.
  • Markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase & bilirubin → Biliary obstruction.

6. Coagulation Studies (PT, INR, PTT)

  • Prolonged PT/INR → Indicates liver dysfunction or anticoagulant use.
  • Platelet count → Needed in suspected DIC, sepsis, or hemorrhage.

7. β-hCG (Pregnancy Test)

  • Must be done in all women of childbearing age to rule out ectopic pregnancy.
B. Urine & Stool Tests
1. Urinalysis
  • Hematuria → Suggests nephrolithiasis, UTI, or trauma.
  • Pyuria → Suggests infection (e.g., pyelonephritis, UTI).
  • Dark urine with bilirubin → Suggests hepatobiliary disease.

2. Stool Tests

  • Occult blood → May indicate gastrointestinal bleeding, ischemic colitis, or malignancy.
  • Stool culture → For infectious diarrhea (Salmonella, Shigella, C. difficile, cholera, etc.).
II. Imaging Studies
A. Chest X-Ray (CXR)
  • Indications:
  • Free air under diaphragm → Perforated viscus.
  • Lower lobe pneumonia → Can mimic acute abdomen.
  • Mediastinal air → Esophageal rupture (Boerhaave’s syndrome).
B. Plain Abdominal X-Ray (AXR)
  • Indications:
  • Suspected bowel obstruction:
    • Dilated bowel loops.
    • Air-fluid levels.
    • Absence of rectal gas.
  • Pneumoperitoneum (free air).
  • Foreign body ingestion.
  • Toxic megacolon (massive colonic dilatation).
  • Calcifications (renal or gallstones).
C. Abdominal Ultrasound (US)
  • Indications:
  • First-line for RUQ pain (biliary pathology)
  • Safe for pregnant patients.
  • May help diagnose:
    • Acute cholecystitis (thickened gallbladder wall, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign).
    • Appendicitis (non-compressible appendix >6mm diameter).
    • Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA >3 cm).
    • Ectopic pregnancy (adnexal mass, free fluid).
    • Pelvic inflammatory disease (thickened fallopian tubes, free fluid).
    • FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) → Evaluates for hemoperitoneum in trauma.
D. Computed Tomography (CT) Scan
  • Indications:
  • Preferred imaging for acute abdomen if diagnosis is unclear.
  • High accuracy for appendicitis, diverticulitis, perforation, and ischemia.
  • IV contrast: Enhances visualization of vascular perfusion.

4. Admission to Medical Service for Non-Surgical Abdominal Pain

Certain medical conditions mimic acute surgical conditions and require medical (rather than surgical) treatment. Misdiagnosing these can lead to unnecessary

surgeries.

  • Gastroenteritis → Crampy pain, diarrhea → Stool cultures.
  • Hepatitis or hepatic abscess → RUQ pain, fever → Liver function tests, ultrasound.
  • Porphyria, sickle cell crisis, Addison’s disease → Episodic pain → Blood tests.

These patients do not require surgery but must be closely monitored by a medical team.

1. Persistent Pain for Over 6 Hours
  • Acute abdominal pain lasting >6 hours should be assumed surgical until proven otherwise.
  • Localized pain and tenderness → High likelihood of a surgical condition.

2. Common Pitfalls & Atypical Presentations
Certain conditions may be missed initially due to their unusual presentation:

  • Appendicitis:

  • Intestinal Obstruction:
  • Early cases may have minimal symptoms.

  • Salpingitis, dysmenorrhea, ovarian cysts, UTIs → Can mimic acute appendicitis.

  • Elderly woman without prior surgery → Consider incarcerated femoral hernia.
  • Gallstone ileus → Recurrent partial obstruction before complete blockage (pneumobilia on imaging).
  • Richter’s hernia → Minimal distension with strangulation risk.

  • Severe pain, minimal tenderness → Suggests mesenteric ischemia.

  • High-risk patients → History of AFib, peripheral vascular disease, recent MI.

Anatomy of the Appendix
Location and Orientation
  • The appendix is a blind-ended, tubular diverticulum that extends from the cecum.
  • In infants, the appendix originates as a conical extension of the cecum.
  • As the cecum expands, the appendix shifts leftward and dorsally, ultimately settling about 2.5 cm below the ileocecal valve.
  • The three taeniae coli of the colon converge at the base of the appendix, providing a useful surgical landmark.
  • The appendix is freely mobile in most adults but may be retrocecal in 16% of cases.
Variability in Positioning

The appendix is highly variable in position, which can influence the presentation of appendicitis:

pain
Pelvic30%Can mimic gynecologic or urinary conditions
Subcecal2%May present with suprapubic pain
Pre-ileal or post- ileal2%May cause diffuse abdominal pain
Blood Supply of the Appendix
  • Appendicular artery (a branch of the ileocolic artery, from the superior mesenteric artery)
  • This end-artery makes the appendix prone to ischemia and necrosis if obstructed.
Lymphatic System of the Appendix
  • The appendix contains abundant lymphoid follicles that appear 2 weeks after birth.
  • The number of lymphoid follicles peaks at ~200 by age 15.
  • With aging, there is progressive atrophy of lymphoid tissue, along with fibrosis of the wall and partial or complete luminal obliteration.
Physiology of the Appendix
Immune Function
  • The appendix is rich in lymphoid tissue, functioning as a secondary lymphoid organ.
  • It contributes to mucosal immunity by promoting antibody production and supporting the gut microbiome.
Role in Gut Microbiome
  • The appendix serves as a reservoir for beneficial gut bacteria, helping to repopulate the colon after diarrhea or infections.
Possible Vestigial Function
  • The appendix may be an evolutionary remnant, but recent studies suggest it plays a role in immune function and gut flora homeostasis.
Clinical Relevance
Appendicitis
  • Obstruction (due to fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia, or tumors) leads to:
  • Luminal distension
  • Bacterial overgrowth
  • Ischemia and necrosis
  • Symptoms depend on appendix location (e.g., RLQ pain in the retrocecal appendix, suprapubic pain in the pelvic appendix).
Appendiceal Tumors
  • Rare but significant causes of appendiceal pathology (e.g., carcinoid tumors, adenocarcinomas, mucinous neoplasms).
Acute Appendicitis
General Considerations
  • Prevalence: Approximately 7% of individuals in Western countries develop acute appendicitis during their lifetime.
  • Incidence: Over 250,000 appendectomies are performed annually in the U.S.
  • Most Common Surgical Emergency: Appendicitis accounts for 1% of all surgical operations.
  • Etiology:
  • Obstruction of the proximal lumen by:
    • Fibrous bands
    • Lymphoid hyperplasia
    • Fecaliths (found in ~10% of cases)
    • Calculi or parasites (rare)
  • Infectious etiology remains uncertain but is suggested by clustering patterns.
Pathophysiology

1. Initial obstruction leads to increased mucosal secretions and intraluminal

  • pressure.

2. Vascular compromise results in ischemia.

3. Bacterial overgrowth and inflammatory response occur.

4. Gangrene and perforation can develop within 24–48 hours if untreated.

Complications of Acute Appendicitis
A. Perforation
  • Occurs in up to 50% of cases in patients <10 or >50 years old.
  • Typically develops after 24–48 hours of untreated appendicitis.
  • Signs of perforation:
  • More severe pain and higher fever (~38.3°C).
  • Generalized peritonitis (if free perforation occurs).
  • Consequences:
  • Increased risk of sepsis and abscess formation.
  • In young women, fourfold increased risk of tubal infertility.
B. Peritonitis
  • Localized peritonitis: Occurs with microscopic perforation or gangrene.
  • Generalized peritonitis: Results from gross perforation.
  • Signs of peritonitis:
  • Severe abdominal distension.
  • Rigid abdomen, absent bowel sounds (ileus).
  • Severe toxicity, tachycardia, and high fever.
  • Treatment:
  • Urgent laparotomy or laparoscopy.
  • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (covering Gram-negative and anaerobes).
  • Aggressive fluid resuscitation.
C. Appendiceal Abscess
  • Occurs when the infection becomes walled off by omentum and adjacent viscera.
  • Presentation:
  • Tender RLQ mass.
  • Fever, leukocytosis.
  • Persistent pain despite antibiotics.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Ultrasound or CT scan to differentiate between abscess and phlegmon.
  • Treatment:
  • Percutaneous image-guided drainage.
  • IV antibiotics.
  • Interval appendectomy (after 6 weeks) if abscess resolves.
D. Pylephlebitis (Septic Thrombophlebitis of the Portal Vein)
  • Rare (<1%) but serious complication.
  • Pathophysiology: Infection spreads via the portal venous system, causing liver abscesses.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Chills, high fever, jaundice.
  • Hepatic abscess formation.
  • Treatment:
  • Immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
  • Possible anticoagulation.
  • Surgical drainage of abscesses.
Prevention of Appendicitis
  • No established preventive strategies.
  • Incidental appendectomy (removal of the appendix during another surgery) is no longer routinely recommended.
  • Management when normal appendix is found during laparoscopy:
  • Some surgeons prefer removal to prevent future appendicitis.
  • Others choose not to remove it, as unnecessary surgery carries risks.
Treatment of Acute Appendicitis
A. Surgical Management
1. Laparoscopic Appendectomy
Preferred surgical approach due to:
  • Less postoperative pain.
  • Faster recovery & shorter hospital stay (by ~1 day).
  • Lower wound infection rate.
  • Better cosmetic outcome.
  • Feasible for both simple and complicated appendicitis.
Challenges:
  • Higher operating costs.
  • Longer operative time.
  • Conversion to open surgery (0–27%) based on patient factors.
2. Open Appendectomy
Indications:
  • Complicated appendicitis (perforation, abscess, peritonitis).
  • Limited access to laparoscopic equipment.
  • Severe adhesions from prior surgeries.
Challenges:
  • Longer recovery.
  • Increased postoperative pain.
  • Higher risk of wound infection.
B. Non-Operative Management (NOM)
Indications:
  • Uncomplicated appendicitis confirmed by CT.
  • High surgical risk (e.g., severe comorbidities).
  • Patient preference.
Antibiotic regimen:
  • IV ceftriaxone + metronidazole, followed by oral antibiotics.
  • Success rate: ~70%.
  • Recurrence rate: ~30%.
Limitations:
  • Delayed perforation risk.
  • 20–30% recurrence within 1 year.
  • No benefit in complicated cases (perforation, abscess, sepsis).

Controversies in Appendicitis Treatment
1. Should Appendectomy Always Be Performed?
  • Traditionally, appendectomy was the only treatment.
  • Now, antibiotic therapy is an option for uncomplicated cases.
  • Surgery remains the gold standard due to lower recurrence rates.
2. Interval Appendectomy for Abscess or Phlegmon?
  • Some surgeons prefer:
  • Conservative management (IV antibiotics, drainage) + interval appendectomy.
  • Lower overall complication rates.
  • Others advocate for immediate appendectomy to shorten disease duration.
3. Duration of Postoperative Antibiotics?
  • For uncomplicated appendicitis: No antibiotics needed after surgery.
  • For perforated appendicitis:
  • Some recommend 4 days of IV antibiotics.
  • Others suggest shorter durations or stopping after source control.
4. Should an Appendicolith Always Be Removed?
  • No consensus.
  • Some cases of appendicolith-associated appendicitis resolve with antibiotics.
  • Surgery is still the preferred treatment if symptomatic.
Tumors of the Appendix
Benign Tumors of the Appendix
  • Incidence: Found in 4.6% of appendix specimens examined microscopically.
  • Types:
  • Carcinoid tumors (most common).
  • Mucocele (non-neoplastic cystic dilation).
  • Usually incidental findings during appendectomy.
Malignant Tumors of the Appendix
1. Carcinoid & Neuroendocrine Tumors
  • Most common primary appendiceal cancer.
  • Location: Typically found at the tip of the appendix.
  • Behavior:
  • Tumors <2 cm: Generally benign, only 3% have lymph node metastases.
  • Tumors >2 cm: Higher risk of malignancy & metastasis.
  • Rarely causes carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, right heart disease).
  • Management:
  • Appendectomy is sufficient if:
    • Tumor is ≤2 cm.
    • No involvement of lymph nodes, mesoappendix, or cecum.
  • Right hemicolectomy is recommended if:
    • Tumor is >2 cm.
    • Mucinous (adenocarcinoid) elements present.
    • Lymph node involvement or mesoappendix/cecal invasion.
  • Prognosis: Recurrence is rare after appropriate surgery.
2. Appendiceal Adenocarcinoma
  • Rare & aggressive form of appendiceal cancer.
  • Often diagnosed late, as it mimics acute appendicitis.
  • Can spread to lymph nodes & peritoneal surfaces.
  • Management:
  • Right hemicolectomy if disease is localized to appendix/lymph nodes.
  • Chemotherapy may be used for metastatic disease.
  • Prognosis:
  • 5-year survival rate:
    • 60% after right hemicolectomy.
    • 20% after appendectomy alone (often includes patients with distant metastases).

3. Appendiceal Mucocele & Pseudomyxoma Peritonei (PMP) A. Appendiceal Mucocele

  • Definition: Cystic dilation of the appendix filled with mucin.
  • Types:
  • Simple mucocele (due to chronic obstruction).
  • Mucinous neoplasm (precancerous or malignant).
  • Management:
  • Appendectomy if no involvement of cecum.
  • Cecal resection if base of appendix is involved.
B. Pseudomyxoma Peritonei (PMP)
  • Definition: Peritoneal spread of mucin-producing tumor cells, leading to mucin accumulation in the abdomen.
  • Caused by:
  • Ruptured mucinous appendiceal tumors.
  • Dissemination of mucinous neoplastic cells.
  • Management:
  • Complete surgical removal of mucin deposits (cytoreductive surgery).
  • Intraperitoneal hyperthermic chemotherapy (HIPEC).
  • Postoperative systemic chemotherapy (if invasive).

  • Types:
  • Mechanical Obstruction (More common) → Extrinsic, intrinsic, or luminal obstruction.
  • Paralytic (Adynamic) Ileus → Loss of peristalsis without obstruction.
2. Etiology
Mechanical SBO (Common Causes)

1. Adhesions (60-75%) - Post-surgical fibrosis.

2. Hernias - Second most common, especially in non-surgical patients.

3. Neoplasms - Tumor-related obstruction.

4. Other Causes:

  • Crohn’s disease (inflammation, strictures).
  • Intussusception (common in children).
  • Volvulus (malrotation or adhesions).
  • Gallstone ileus (from cholecystoduodenal fistula).
  • Foreign bodies (e.g., bezoars).
Paralytic Ileus (Non-Mechanical)
  • Postoperative ileus (common after abdominal surgery).
  • Electrolyte imbalance (hypokalemia).
  • Drugs (opioids, anticholinergics).
  • Intra-abdominal inflammation (pancreatitis, peritonitis).
  • Sepsis or shock.
3. Pathophysiology
  • Proximal bowel distention → Fluid accumulation → Increased intraluminal pressure.
  • Venous compression → Ischemia → Necrosis → Perforation → Peritonitis.
  • Bacterial translocation → Septic shock (in strangulated bowel).
  • Strangulation progresses faster than simple obstruction.
4. Clinical Presentation
Symptoms
  • Colicky abdominal pain (mechanical obstruction).
  • Diffuse, constant pain (paralytic ileus).
  • Nausea & vomiting:
  • Early, non-bilious (proximal SBO).
  • Late, feculent (distal SBO).
  • Obstipation (absence of flatus/stool).
  • Abdominal distension (more in distal obstruction).
Signs
  • Tachycardia & hypotension (dehydration).
  • High-pitched bowel sounds (early) → Absent sounds (late)
  • Surgical scars, hernias (clue to cause).
  • Peritoneal signs (rebound tenderness, guarding) → Suggests strangulation.
5. Diagnosis
Lab Findings
  • Leukocytosis (infection/ischemia).
  • Elevated hematocrit (dehydration).
  • Metabolic alkalosis (from vomiting).
  • Lactic acidosis (suggests bowel ischemia).
Imaging
1. Abdominal X-ray (1st-line test)
  • Dilated loops of bowel (>3 cm).
  • Air-fluid levels in a "ladder-like" pattern.
  • Minimal colonic gas (suggests SBO).

2. CT scan (Gold Standard)

  • Identifies transition point & strangulation signs:
    • Bowel wall thickening.
    • Pneumatosis (air in bowel wall).
    • Portal venous gas (suggests necrosis).

3. Gastrografin Study (Water-Soluble Contrast)

  • If no contrast reaches colon within 24 hrs → Predicts need for surgery.
6. Differential Diagnosis
  • Paralytic ileus: Diffuse bowel dilation, no peristalsis, often post-op.
  • Colonic obstruction: Large bowel dilation, possible competent ileocecal valve.
  • Acute mesenteric ischemia: Severe pain, metabolic acidosis, high lactate.
  • Gastroenteritis: Vomiting & diarrhea, but no distension.
  • Pseudo-obstruction: Intestinal motility disorder (e.g., scleroderma, amyloidosis).
7. Treatment
Initial Management (All Patients)
  • Fluid Resuscitation - IV fluids, correct electrolytes.
  • Nasogastric (NG) Tube - Decompress stomach, prevent aspiration.
  • Bowel Rest - NPO (nothing by mouth).
  • Urinary Catheter - Monitor hydration status.
Non-Surgical Treatment (80% Improve)
  • Adhesive SBO: Most resolve with conservative care (IV fluids, NG decompression).
  • Postoperative Ileus: Supportive care, mobilization, gum chewing.
Indications for Surgery
  • Signs of strangulation (ischemia, necrosis, peritonitis, perforation).
  • Persistent SBO after 48 hours of conservative treatment.
  • Closed-loop obstruction or complete obstruction on imaging.
Surgical Options
  • Adhesiolysis (for adhesions).
  • Hernia repair (if incarcerated).
  • Bowel resection (if necrosis).
  • Bypass or stoma (if unresectable tumor or carcinomatosis).
8. Prognosis
  • 80% of SBO due to adhesions resolve without surgery.
  • Mortality:
  • Simple obstruction: <5%.
  • Strangulated obstruction:
    • 8% if operated within 36 hours.
    • 25% if delayed beyond 36 hours.

1. General Overview
  • Definition: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease affecting any part of the GI tract, most commonly the terminal ileum.
  • Epidemiology:
  • Highest incidence in North America & Europe.
  • Peak onset: 15-25 years.
  • Genetic risk: 6-10x higher in first-degree relatives.

  • Genetic predisposition (CARD15/NOD2 gene mutation).

Acute Mesenteric Ischemia (AMI)
1. Overview & Pathophysiology
  • Definition: A life-threatening condition due to reduced blood flow to the small intestine, leading to ischemia and necrosis if untreated.
  • Types & Causes: 1. Arterial embolism (50%):
    • Most common cause.
    • Source: Cardiac emboli (atrial fibrillation, endocarditis, post- MI).
    • Sudden, severe pain out of proportion to exam.
  • 2. Acute arterial thrombosis (25%):
    • Seen in atherosclerosis, vasculitis, or connective tissue disorders.
    • Gradual onset, worsening postprandial pain.
  • 3. Nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia (20%):
    • Seen in ICU patients, shock, vasopressor use.
    • Diffuse vasoconstriction leads to ischemia.
  • 4. Mesenteric venous thrombosis (5%):
    • Hypercoagulable states, portal hypertension, sepsis, trauma.
    • Slower progression with nausea, diarrhea, dull pain.
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Ischemia → Loss of intestinal barrier → Bacterial translocation.
  • Reperfusion injury → Oxidative stress → Further tissue damage.
  • Sepsis & Multi-organ Failure in late stages.
2. Clinical Presentation
A. Symptoms
  • Severe, sudden onset abdominal pain (most commonly embolic).
  • Pain out of proportion to physical exam.
  • Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.
  • Bloody stools (late sign).
  • Shock & peritonitis (indicate infarction).
B. Physical Exam
  • Early: Mild or no tenderness despite severe pain.
  • Late: Guarding, rebound tenderness, peritonitis (suggest bowel infarction).
3. Diagnosis
A. Laboratory Tests
  • ↑ WBC count (>15,000/mm³)
  • ↑ Lactate (metabolic acidosis)
  • ↑ Amylase & CK (intestinal infarction)
  • ↑ D-dimer (suggestive of thrombosis)
B. Imaging
  • Abdominal X-ray:
  • Late signs: Bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas.
  • CT Angiography (CTA) → First-line test:
  • Identifies vascular occlusion, bowel ischemia, infarction.
  • Preferred for venous thrombosis.
  • Mesenteric Angiography (Gold Standard for arterial causes):
  • Identifies emboli, thrombi, vasospasm.
  • Allows catheter-based intervention (thrombectomy, vasodilators).
  • Duplex Ultrasound:
  • Limited role (affected by bowel gas).
  • MRI/MRA:
  • Alternative for renal-impaired patients (gadolinium contrast).
4. Treatment
A. Initial Management
  • NPO (nothing by mouth)
  • Aggressive IV fluids (crystalloid resuscitation)
  • IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (to prevent bacterial translocation)
  • IV heparin (for venous thrombosis)
  • Pain control (avoid vasoconstrictive agents like vasopressors)

B. Definitive Treatment 1. Arterial Embolism

  • Surgical embolectomy (via open laparotomy) = Standard of care.
  • Endovascular catheter-directed thrombolysis (in hemodynamically stable patients without peritonitis).
  • Assess bowel viability → Resection if necrotic.
2. Acute Arterial Thrombosis
  • Surgical bypass (e.g., saphenous vein graft) or endovascular stenting.
  • Thrombectomy alone is NOT sufficient (high re-occlusion rates).
3. Nonocclusive Mesenteric Ischemia (NOMI)
  • Treat underlying cause (discontinue vasopressors, increase cardiac output).
  • Intra-arterial papaverine infusion (vasodilator) via angiography.
4. Mesenteric Venous Thrombosis
  • Systemic anticoagulation (IV heparin, then oral anticoagulation for 6 months).
  • Surgery only if infarction or peritonitis.
5. Prognosis & Outcomes
  • High mortality (30-60%) due to delayed diagnosis.
  • Poor prognosis if bowel infarction has occurred.
  • 5-year survival: 18-50%.
  • Better outcomes in venous thrombosis vs arterial ischemia.
  • Early diagnosis & intervention are critical to survival.
